*[reasoning in my own voice]*

I've worked this land for fifty years now, since before they broke up the collectives. It's just me and the old lady at home — the children went to the city long ago, they send money sometimes but they won't come back to farm. We've got 5 mu, which is enough for two old people. Some grain to eat, some to sell, a bit of cotton money in the fall.

I split the land like I always do. Three mu I do wheat then maize, same as most everyone in the village. The other two mu is cotton — we've grown cotton on that piece for years, the soil suits it and the price has been alright. I'm too old to change things much. What worked before still works.

For the wheat, I plant around the cold dew, early October. I buy the regular seed from the agro-shop in town, nothing special — the same kind my neighbor Old Wang uses. Before planting I spread compound fertilizer, about two bags for the three mu (that's roughly one bag per 1.5 mu). After the spring green-up I topdress urea, maybe half a bag per mu. If the wheat looks yellow at jointing I'll add a bit more, but usually I don't. I water three times: once after planting if the ground is dry, once at green-up, once at heading. The well is metered now so I can't waste it. For harvest I pay the combine man — 50 yuan per mu, but it's quick, what would I do, cut three mu by hand at my age?

For maize, the window is very tight — I have to plant within a week of cutting the wheat. I rent the no-till seeder from the village. Drop the seed and one round of compound fertilizer at the same time, then I'm done with fertilizer for maize. If it rains I don't irrigate at all; if July is dry I'll water once, maybe twice. Spray once for weeds early on. The maize harvest is in late September, again the machine.

Cotton is more work and that's the trouble — picking takes weeks and it's just the two of us. I plant late April after the soil warms. Less fertilizer than the grain crops; cotton doesn't want too much nitrogen or it grows leaves instead of bolls. Spray a few times in summer for the bollworm — can't skip that or you lose everything. We pick by hand from September through October, sometimes my daughter comes for a few days to help.

I don't keep books. I know roughly what things cost and what I'll get back. As long as we have enough to eat and a little money for the doctor, that's good enough.
